title: On the ring, a key belongs to the first server clockwise from it
caption: Servers and keys share one hash space 0–99 bent into a circle, read clockwise from the top. Labels give ring positions; spacing is for readability.

steps.text: Hash every server name onto the ring: A at 20, B at 50, C at 85. Hash every key onto the same ring.
Keys at 25 and 36 walk clockwise and meet B at 50 first, so B owns them.
Keys at 58, 63 and 74 meet C at 85.
Key 91 walks past 99, wraps to 0, and meets A at 20, together with keys 8 and 17. Each server owns the arc that ends at it.

scenarios.name: Remove server B
scenarios.summary: Only B's keys move, all to its clockwise neighbour C. Nothing else changes, but C now carries two arcs and may be the next to fall.
scenarios.caption: Without B, its arc (20, 50] merges into C's: the keys there walk on to 85.

steps.text: Server B crashes and is removed from the ring.
Keys at 25 and 36 walk clockwise past where B was and meet C at 85.
Keys owned by A and C don't move: no mass reshuffle, unlike hash % N.
But C now owns everything from 20 to 85, most of the ring. With one point per server the whole load lands on one neighbour.

scenarios.name: Risk: uneven arcs
scenarios.summary: With one hashed point per server, arc lengths are random: one server can own several times the keys of another. Virtual nodes even it out.
scenarios.caption: Here B happened to hash to 32, just after A: its arc is tiny and C's is huge.

steps.text: Positions come from a hash, so nobody chooses them. Say B lands at 32 instead of 50.
B owns only (20, 32]: 12% of the ring and one key.
C owns (32, 85]: 53% of the ring, more than four times B's share. Its memory and CPU fill first.
Fix: give each server 100–200 virtual points so every share averages out close to 1/N.
